usage: at the start of the month
에 marks the time point; this is the default way to say 'in early-month'
이번 달(this month) pins down which month's beginning you mean
from the beginning of the month
부터 marks the starting edge of a stretch of time
to get one's salary at the start of the month
Classic collocation — payday talk almost always uses 월초/월말
examples: 월초예요.
It's the beginning of the month.
월초 is a noun, so it takes 예요 — say 월초예요, never 월초이에요
저는 보통 월초에 안 바빠요.
I'm usually not busy at the start of the month.
Time word + 에 sets the 'when'; 보통(usually) fits routine talk
월초부터 돈을 아끼기로 했어요.
I decided to start saving money from the beginning of the month.
Real-life resolution: 월초부터 frames a fresh start
nuance: 월초 is Sino-Korean 月初, literally 'month-beginning', and means roughly the first third or first few days of a month — not pinpoint day 1 (that is 1일). Its mirror image is 월말 月末 'month-end', and the two are habitually said as a pair: 월초엔 여유롭고 월말엔 쪼들려요. The nearest contrast is 초순, which is more formal/written and means the first ten days specifically (초순/중순/하순 split the month in thirds); 월초 is the everyday spoken word. Note that here 초 means 'beginning/early', a completely different 초 from 초(秒) 'second' of time or 초(醋) 'vinegar' — same sound, unrelated. The English-speaker trap is twofold: (1) spacing — write it solid as 월초, never 월 초; and (2) the particle — English says 'in early month' but Korean says 월초에 with 에, and to say 'it IS the start of the month' you need the noun-copula 월초예요, not a verb.

mistakes: Writing 월 초 with a space — it is a single fixed word, 월초.

usage: at the end of the month
에 marks the time point — the standard way to say 'late in the month'
by the end of the month
까지 sets a deadline; very common with bills and work due dates
이번 달 fixes which month's end you mean
정산(settling accounts) is a textbook business pairing
examples: 월말이에요.
It's the end of the month.
월말 ends in a consonant (ㄹ), so the copula is the full 이에요
월말까지 돈을 내야 해요.
I have to pay by the end of the month.
까지 = the deadline 'by'; pairs naturally with 내다(to pay)
월말이라 통장이 텅 비었어요.
It's month-end, so my account is totally empty.
Lived-in complaint: -이라(서) gives the reason, 텅 비다 = be empty
nuance: 월말 is Sino-Korean 月末, literally 'month-end', the last stretch of the month and the exact opposite of 월초 月初 'month-beginning'; Koreans reflexively say the two together (월초엔 풍족, 월말엔 빈곤). Its more formal near-synonym is 하순, the final ten days specifically, paired with 초순/중순 in the 초·중·하순 system — 월말 is the casual spoken word while 하순 reads as written/news Korean. A key boundary: 말(末) means the 'end/closing part' of a period, so it attaches to time spans — 월말, 연말(year-end), 주말(weekend), 학기말(end of term). Do NOT swap in 끝, which is the everyday word for the physical/abstract end of an object or event (줄 끝 'end of the line', 영화 끝 'end of the movie'); '월끝' is simply not a word. The English-speaker pitfall is also the particle: 'at the end of the month' is 월말에, and a deadline 'by month-end' is 월말까지 — picking 에 vs 까지 changes the meaning from 'when' to 'no later than'.

Writing 월 말 with a space — it is one word, 월말.
Using 월말에 when you mean a deadline — 'pay by month-end' needs 월말까지, not 월말에.

usage: 결혼(marriage) + 기념일, written solid as one word
Korean couples count days; '백일' is read 'baegil'
to look after / not forget an anniversary
챙기다 is THE verb for remembering and honoring special days
깜빡하다 = to blank out / slip one's mind — the classic relationship sin
examples: 오늘 우리 기념일이에요.
Today is our anniversary.
기념일 ends in a consonant, so 이에요; 우리 = our
기념일에 꽃을 선물했어요.
I gave flowers as a gift on the anniversary.
에 marks the day; 선물하다(to give as a gift) fits the occasion
결혼기념일을 깜빡해서 아내한테 혼났어요.
I forgot our wedding anniversary, so my wife told me off.
Real-life scene: -아서 gives the cause, 혼나다 = to get scolded
nuance: 기념일 is Sino-Korean 紀念日, literally 'commemorate-day' (紀念 'to commemorate' + 日 'day'), so it is any date you deliberately mark each year. In daily life it skews strongly toward romance — couples celebrate 100일, 200일 and the 1주년 'first anniversary' as 기념일 — but it equally covers a company's 창립기념일 'founding anniversary' or a national 기념일. Keep three relatives apart: 명절 is a traditional seasonal holiday (설날, 추석); 공휴일 is a public day off on the calendar; 기념일 is a personally or institutionally meaningful date, which may or may not be a day off. The English-speaker pitfall is glossing it as 'memorial day' — that pulls the somber English sense, whereas 기념일 is usually happy/celebratory (a true solemn memorial is 추모일 or 추도식). Natural verbs are 기념일을 챙기다 'to honor it' and 기념일을 깜빡하다 'to forget it'; and because 기념일 ends in a consonant, the copula is the full 이에요, never 예요.

usage: the first day of the trip
Noun + 첫날 with a space between them; 여행 첫날 is a stock pairing
the first day at a new job
출근(going to work) + 첫날 — the nervous first day at work
부터 stresses 'starting from the very first day'
Fixed idiom — 첫날밤 specifically means the newlyweds' first night
examples: 오늘이 첫날이에요.
Today is the first day.
첫날 ends in ㄹ, so the copula is 이에요
여행 첫날에 비가 왔어요.
It rained on the first day of the trip.
에 marks the day; note the noun phrase 여행 첫날 is written with a space
출근 첫날부터 실수를 해서 너무 창피했어요.
I made a mistake on my very first day at work, so I was so embarrassed.
Lived-in scene: 첫날부터 = 'from day one', -아서 gives the cause
nuance: 첫날 fuses the native-Korean ordinal 첫 'first(-ever)' with 날 'day', so it means the very first day of some bounded thing — a trip, a job, school, a vacation. The crucial contrast is 첫 vs 처음: 첫 is a pre-noun modifier that attaches directly to a noun (첫날, 첫사랑 'first love', 첫인상 'first impression'), while 처음 is a free noun/adverb meaning 'the beginning / at first' (처음에는 'at first'). So 'first day' is 첫날, and the very natural-sounding but wrong '처음 날' is something learners must unlearn. Two more boundary notes: spacing — 첫날 is written solid as one word, but when another noun precedes it you DO put a space (여행 첫날, not 여행첫날); and pronunciation — the patchim makes 첫날 sound like [천날] through nasal assimilation. Beware also the fixed idiom 첫날밤 'wedding night', which is not simply 'the first night' literally. Since 첫날 ends in a consonant (ㄹ), the copula is 이에요.

usage: at the end of the year
에 marks the time point; the default way to say 'late in the year'
Set four-character phrase 年末年始 covering late Dec through early Jan
모임(gathering) — December is packed with these
정산 — the annual income-tax reconciliation every worker dreads/awaits
examples: 벌써 연말이에요.
It's already the end of the year.
연말 ends in a consonant, so 이에요; 벌써(already) fits the surprised tone
연말에 가족이랑 여행을 가요.
I'm going on a trip with my family at the end of the year.
에 marks the time; 이랑 = casual 'with'
연말이라 약속이 너무 많아서 정신이 없어요.
It's year-end, so I have way too many plans and I'm swamped.
Real-life: -이라(서) 'because it's', 정신이 없다 = to be frazzled
nuance: 연말 is Sino-Korean 年末, literally 'year-end', meaning roughly December and the closing of the year; its opposite is 연초 年初 'year-beginning' (early January), and the two pair up just like 월초/월말 do. The 말(末) here is the very same 'end/closing' element found in 월말(month-end), 주말(weekend) and 학기말(end of term) — a reliable building block. A frequent confusion is 연말 vs 월말: 연(年) is 'year' and 월(月) is 'month', so 연말 = end of the YEAR while 월말 = end of the MONTH; mixing the hanja flips the scale entirely. Culturally, 연말 evokes a busy, festive rush — 송년회 'year-end parties', 모임, gift-giving — captured in the set phrase 연말연시 年末年始 'year-end and new-year', and in the workplace 연말정산 'year-end tax settlement'. The English-speaker pitfalls: don't say 끝 ('연끝' is not a word — 말 is the fixed bound morpheme for time-spans), use 연말에 with 에 for 'at year-end', and since 연말 ends in a consonant the copula is 이에요, not 예요.
